title: What If Snakes Bit You 200 Times? Scientists Wanted One Man's Blood

scenes.text: What if you let deadly snakes bite you 200 times? One man did. Scientists wanted his blood.
Starting around 2000, an American snake collector injected himself with venom more than 650 times.
He took real bites too: cobras, taipans, black mambas. Early on, two cobra bites left him in a coma for four days.
After 18 years, his blood carried antibodies that recognize toxins shared by many snakes.
In 2025, researchers combined two of them with a drug and tested the mix on mice, against venom from 19 species.
It fully protected against 13 and partly against the other six. Nobody should ever copy him. But his blood could change how antivenom is made.

description:
What if you let some of the world's deadliest snakes bite you 200 times?
One American man did. Between about 2000 and 2018 he was bitten more than 200 times and injected himself with venom more than 650 times, 856 exposures in all, from cobras, taipans, black mambas and other snakes; early on, two cobra bites put him in a coma for four days. Researchers at the company Centivax and Columbia University isolated antibodies from his blood and, in a study published in Cell in May 2025, combined two of them with the drug varespladib. In mice, the cocktail gave full protection against venom from 13 of 19 dangerous elapid species and partial protection against the other six. It does not yet cover vipers and has not been tested in people. The WHO estimates snakebite kills up to 138,000 people a year, and today's antivenoms are made by immunising animals such as horses. Doctors stress that nobody should try this.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The next step is testing it on snake-bitten dogs in Australia. Which animal's defences would you want to borrow?
